segments.text: Hello and welcome to The Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, having a hip or knee replacement when you're relatively young. What should you know?
Surprising genetic findings in women with endometriosis, which could change the treatment.
And we'll follow up last week's story on outdoor temperatures and the chances of developing gestational diabetes in a minute.
A hormone that's commonly used to speed up labour turns out to have quite profound effects on the brain and behaviour.
The hormone is called oxytocin, and when given by a nasal spray to children with autism
in a trial at the Brain and Mind Centre at the University of Sydney,
it showed significant benefits in their behaviour.
Those findings have launched a series of international collaborations
which hold a lot of hope for children with autism.
Professor Adam Guastella, who is one of the research leaders at the Brain and Mind Centre,
is in our Sydney studio. Welcome.
Welcome, Norman.
So, just tell us why oxytocin, which causes the uterus to contract,
has evolved in orgasm and things like that.
involved in behaviour? Well, let me just start with autism first, actually. As you're no doubt
aware, autism is a neurodevelopmental disability that weakens one's ability to process and respond
accurately to social relationships and social information. So people with autism can often be
seen to have difficulty with eye gaze and recognising emotion and expressing one's
own emotions and understanding the nuances of social information. And that often gets worse
as the information becomes more complex, such as group situations.
And there's a brain process underlying some of these developments,
and we're starting to understand some of the brain processes
that are really underpinning these difficulties.
So oxytocin?
So oxytocin is a hormone and a neuropeptide,
and there's been 30 years of research demonstrating...
Neuropeptide meaning it's a short protein,
which you're suggesting acts as a messenger in the brain.
That's right.
Rather than a traditional hormone.
Yeah, that's right.
And we know that when, I'll just go straight to the neurobiological research, that oxytocin
facilitates communication and in particular facilitates the processing of social information.
So it seems to facilitate the processing of faces, memory for faces, ability to respond
to faces accurately.
We've conducted over 10 years of research in humans showing that when we administer
the nasal spray, it improves things like eye gaze, emotion recognition and memory for
social information.
In non-autistic human?
in students that we've tested as well as people with autism who are adults.
So tell me about this trial you did.
We'd spent 10 years studying the potential of the treatment and then we administered oxytocin
morning and night for five weeks to young children with autism aged between three and
eight years of age.
So these are kids with serious communication disorders, intellectual disability and so
on, the full bit.
Absolutely.
Not at the other end of the autism spectrum where they might just have some communication
problems.
Autism is a spectrum.
they all met what we call the diagnosis of autism, and some were more severe than others,
but they all met the diagnosis. But we certainly didn't just select those that were not severe,
which is common in a lot of research. So with these children, we asked caregivers to give the
oxytocin morning and night, and we also asked the caregivers at a separate time to give placebo
morning and night for five weeks. And what we found was really quite interesting.
And they didn't know it was a placebo. No one knew. It was a double-blind,
randomised trial. And what we found was that when children received the oxytocin,
they were more responsive. They were better able to respond to their caregivers. Caregivers noticed
this social engagement or increased social engagement. And even when they came into the
laboratory, when we did our social testing, the experimenters in our research study who didn't
know who received what also reported that the children under oxytocin showed improved social
behavior. And oxytocin doesn't last long in the blood. So when they stopped it, they went back to
where they were? Well, you know, this is speaking to the mechanism. So it's really very, very
interesting. In this study, when people stop the oxytocin treatment, they went back to where they
were. That's correct. But what we think oxytocin can do is open up a window of opportunity to teach
social skills and social rules for young children so they can respond more effectively to early
intervention. So I think you're doing a study now with Duke University in North Carolina,
where you're combining oxytocin with an intensive training program.
Yeah, that's right. So presently, the best treatment for autism in young children
is social learning therapies like Early Start Denver model. And these therapies are most
effective when provided to young children aged between two and five.
And they've been credited with stopping the stereotypic behaviour. We've got the kid in
the corner banging their head and that sort of thing that they really try and bring a child
back into mainstream.
That's right. They can be more socially engaged and in some ways find the social experience a
lot more enjoyable. Now, some children respond to these therapies and some don't. They get
reasonably good outcomes, but all children in Australia should have access to those therapies,
but we need to improve response. And so what we're doing now is we're looking at if we combine these
very critical windows of opportunity with oxytocin treatment and enhance the learning,
whether that produces a stronger response. And what about the, I would hesitate to call it
milder end. I always get talked about people who deal with autism that shouldn't call it milder end
because it can be very disabling, but kids who are more engaged and less disabled by their autism,
does oxytocin help them? Do we know? Well, the focus of our research is on helping people that
want the treatment. We know that in people at the higher end, oxytocin improves social
responsiveness and improves their ability to understand social cues. But really where we want
to go to is that if treatments are effective, we want to be able to provide those treatments. And
when they stop being effective, we need to be able to know, we need to be able to see that
those treatments are no longer effective and switch them to something else.
What do it cost?
It's currently under research. So it's not something that's administered widely
under drug companies in Australia. But as the research develops, it's something that is
regarded as a generic and could be widely available to Australians.
And side effects?
So the research needs to be conducted. I'd never suggest anyone start using oxytocin now,
But in the studies we've conducted, there's been no long-term side effects that we've identified at this point.
You get problems with excess urination and things like that.
So in a small number of, say, three of our participants, we noticed excess urination.
And briefly, some people, you know, it's kind of the thing of the moment.
So people are suggesting oxytocin as an anxiety drug and other things.
Can you comment on that, how widely this could be used?
Well, the mechanisms of oxytocin are important.
So it improves your ability to process social information.
and so for people who might be anxious in social situations they've started to ask well could we
use oxytocin for that purpose it doesn't have a strong anxiolytic property so in the doses that
we provide we don't see very strong anxiolytic effects but it's yeah it's been proposed as a
potential treatment for a range of problems I guess. So when you have the results from your
American collaboration you might have a as you say a useful lever to help these kids and their
families. Yeah I think the key really is that we need to be able to do the large trials here in
Sydney and develop the evidence so that people can have the option of using these sorts of
treatments in the future. Adam, Luke, thanks very much for coming in to join us on The Health Report.
Thank you. Professor Adam Guastella from the Brain and Mind Centre at the University of Sydney.
Let's go to that follow-up to last week's story. You're listening, by the way, to The Health Report
here on RN, ABC News and CBC Radio across Canada. And I'm Norman Swan. So last week,
we had a story on outdoor temperatures and the chances of developing gestational diabetes,
pregnancy-induced diabetes.
It was a Canadian study which effectively showed a doubling of the prevalence
between the depths of winter and the heat of summer in Toronto.
The explanation was that the cold of winter induced brown fat,
which burned calories and made insulin work better in these women.
Well, there's been a similar Australian study which has made equivalent findings
in terms of seasonality of pregnancy,
but the researchers reckon there's a more mundane but so significant explanation.
I have one on the line from Wollongong in New South Wales,
Professor Bob Moses, who's Director of Diabetes Services there.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Thank you, Norman.
So just briefly, the study and what you found.
Well, it goes back more than 20 years that we did an original study
looking at the potential seasonality of gestational problems
using then the current criteria for the diagnosis.
And we found that the glucose levels after the challenge went up, but not enough to cause any change in the prevalence.
We subsequently went on to do work with a climate chamber with the University of Wollongong,
and that we put otherwise healthy people into a climate chamber and gave them a GTT, a glucose tolerance test.
and we found quite a dramatic increase in the one and two hour glucose levels
between 25 and 30 degrees.
So that's been a bit quiet now for some time
and then because the criteria for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes
has changed relatively recently.
In other words, they've lowered the threshold,
it's easier to diagnose it in some ways, easy to qualify.
Or over-diagnosis, perhaps, who knows.
But certainly the criteria have changed and there's now a greater prevalence.
So we decided to, and I must be correct, like most things we do, the nurses told us first
they were having troubles coping with the workload.
Always listen to the nurses.
Yes, having troubles coping with the workload.
So what did you find?
Well, we looked at the criteria prospectively, the number of patients, and we found there
was a marked variation in the prevalence between winter and summer.
With more being in summer.
Yes, so compared to the autumn or spring, there was about 25% more women with abnormal results in summer and 25% less in winter.
So the overall variation was about 50%.
So the Canadians said, well, the reason for that is probably that you're making insulin more efficient in winter because you're producing more brown fat.
But you don't agree with that conclusion?
I don't think any of us have got down that far as to what the possible reason is.

And certainly, as I mentioned before, with a climate chamber and controlling the ambient temperature from 20 through to 35 degrees, there was a dramatic increase in the glucose levels, not the fasting, but the one and two hour levels, starting at 25 to 30 degrees.
But you think it could be a mistake in the way you're measuring, not a mistake, but an aberration in the way blood is shunted around the body that might produce the result?
Well, as you say, it's not a mistake.
The actual rise in the glucose level
was correlated with the core temperature.
And what happens as you get into a hotter environment
is that you tend to divert more blood
from the arterial side to the venous side
so it can help to lose heat through the skin.
And why should that affect your blood sugar?
Because there's more glucose in the arterial side
than in the glucose than in the venous side
because it hasn't gone through the small arterioles and things.
So in other words, what you're suggesting,
and I saw it in your paper,
is that you could actually be over-diagnosing in summer.
So it's not so much that there's more gestational diabetes,
it's just that the way you do the test in that hotter temperature
could actually give you a false positive result.
Or a false negative in winter,
so that there is a 50% range.
Not very comforting, Professor Moses.
Well, I mean, we're about to embark with a climate chamber again,
looking at how long you have to be at a certain temperature
before you don't have this problem.
It might be two hours or three hours,
but that, of course, could be a first world problem.
You have to have air conditioning, et cetera.
On the other hand, if you go to places where this is not sort of practical,
or you may have to devise a correction factor
to try and work out what the proper GTT...
So what's a pregnant woman to do in the interim
while you're working it out?
Well, I think that she should have her normal GTT
at about 24 to 26 weeks
and then possibly discuss the results
with whoever is looking after her.
And work it out from there.
And we're sure to have you on
when you've got some more results from your chamber.
Otherwise, we can sort of rest in our belief
for the moment anyway
that brown fat may actually help you, but thanks for joining us.
It's a pleasure.
Professor Bob Moses is Director of the Diabetes Service
at Illawarra and Shoheaven Local Health District.
That's based in Wollongong.
Endometriosis is an incredibly common problem in women
during their childbearing years.
It's hard to treat, causes infertility and a lot of pain.
Here's Olivia's story.
It took nine years for Olivia to be diagnosed.
First odd occurrence was getting my period at 10 years old,
which is quite young.
It was around about when I was 14 that I started to notice that I was suffering a lot more than the girls in my school.
I thought maybe I was a bit of a sook because I realised that I was having to take time off school
and I was bleeding for a lot longer and I was getting a lot of iron issues
and, you know, my friends would come up to me at school and say,
oh, exercise really helps for period cramps.
And the first thing I thought was the last thing I can do at that time of the month is exercise.
I can't move, I can't get out of bed and that's when I started to think that there was something wrong.
So I started going to the doctors as soon as I got heavy periods
and they were always saying no, it's totally normal, it's fine, I'm sure it's not that bad,
I'm sure it's just a bad month and I just listened to them as a young girl
wanting to sort of fix the issue rather than create more issues.
But it wasn't until early last year that I got extraordinarily bad and the pains were insane
and I started fainting quite regularly and bled for about 10 weeks at a time and I thought no
this isn't normal and so I pushed and pushed and pushed at several doctors and finally got
referred to a gynecologist who agreed and said yep you sound like textbook endometriosis so
then you need to have an operation to formally diagnose it which is called a laparoscopy
and you can choose a surgeon who is either an excision specialist
or just a regular gynaecologist.
I would recommend an excision specialist
because they know how to look for endometriosis.
And if it is, then usually during that operation they will cut it out
or burn it, called excision or ablation,
and go from there, which is hormone therapy
or a plethora of other options,
depending on what your gynaecologist suggests.
Olivia, who spoke to Joel Werner,
As a result of recent genetic research, though, some women with endometriosis may have more effective options.
For a condition with a very low risk of cancer, a North American group has found, surprisingly, a set of cancer genes in endometriosis lesions.
One of the team was Paul Young, who's a gynecologist who specializes in endometriosis at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.
One in ten women of reproductive age have endometriosis. That's approximately one million women in Canada.
And 50% of women who have infertility have endometriosis?
Yes, approximately half of women with infertility,
approximately half of women with troublesome pelvic pain have endometriosis.
So how does a woman know she's got endometriosis? What's the story?
The symptoms include painful menstrual cramps,
also painful sexual activity, painful bowel movements.
The latter often are worse at the time of the period.
There can also be pain that's there even daily.
and then a history of infertility can also be suggestive.
And the pain is mostly in the pelvis?
Mostly in the pelvis, yes.
And what's going on here is that tissue from the uterus, from the womb,
gets seeded throughout the pelvis and sometimes throughout the bowel.
Yes.
And we don't know very much about it apart from the fact that once a woman goes through many pauls,
it tends to go away.
That is correct.
Yeah, it seems to be an estrogen-dependent disease.
And where are we at with treatment for endometriosis?
Because there's not just one type.
treatment is primarily hormonal or surgical hormonal includes progestin-based therapies
such as the birth control pill or progesterone only treatments and then surgery involves excision
or ablation of lesions or hysterectomy and there are two kinds mainly two kinds of lesion here
with endometrial sarum there are ones which are a bit superficial and attached to tissues
and a type where it really burrows into the organ that it attaches itself to which which is a bit
like cancer except that it's not cancer. Correct, that's exactly it. That latter type has tumor-like
qualities but it's most definitely benign and extremely rare for the quote deep infiltrating
type of endometriosis to be associated with cancer. Is there any relationship at all between
endometriosis and cancer? There is a relationship that appears with endometriosis that grows on the

a two to four fold increase in risk. But because endometriosis is so common, only a very tiny
fraction of women with endometriosis develop cancer. And what do we know about what causes
it or the risk factors that put a woman at risk of endometriosis? There seems to be some factors
based on ethnicity, for example, and there's gene changes that one inherits. There could potentially
be dietary factors or other environmental factors. Such as? A lot of them are not in a total confirmed
states, so I would hesitate to say for sure. And the ethnic groups? It's thought that Caucasians
may have a higher rate of endometriosis. So this was a genetic study. Now, you talked about inherited
genes there that might put you at added risk, but this is a study not of inherited genes,
but of the genes that might be mutated in women with endometriosis, particularly this deep
infiltrating kind. Yes. It's something new to the endometriosis itself. Yes. Small study,
but tell us briefly what you found. What we found is that this subtype of endometriosis,
the cells contain gene changes or mutations in certain genes that have been seen to be involved
in certain type of cancer. So these are gene mutations that are thought to drive cancer cell
growth or invasion. So we found these same gene mutations in endometriosis, the deep infiltrating
subtype. So again, this subtype is very rare to become cancer. So what we think is that these gene
mutations may be driving how endometriosis cells can grow or become invasive in some areas. And
that could fundamentally change management. Now, there's quite a spread, though, in these
mutations. It wasn't consistent. It wasn't the same mutation in every woman. Correct. Yes,
it differed between individuals. Why might that be? That's a really good question. It's not
completely clear. I think one factor is that the technologies for detecting these mutations
are evolving, and we think that there'll be even more mutations detected with more sensitive
techniques. The other factor is that although there are several different genes seen,
all of them potentially confer an advantage on the cells to be able to grow.
Now, in cancer, you get these mutations because of environmental factors. Sorry to keep on coming
back to this. So, for example, in melanoma, where some of these mutations occur, it's sunlight.
In colon cancer, it could be red meat or toxins in the bowel.
In the lung, it can be tobacco smoke or unknown environmental factors.
It's going to be an environmental factor that induces these mutations in the endometriosis, surely.
Yeah, I think that is a fantastic point.
And I think definitely more work is needed to find if there's environmental factors that are involving mutations or help these cells in mutations survive longer.
There's a different study that looked at some other benign conditions
that carry these type of mutations,
and they found that age, so increased age was a factor,
and I believe smoking was also a factor,
but I don't think that can be extrapolated to endometriosis.
No, because it's a young woman's disease.
And finally, at least one of these mutations, the KRAS gene,
has drugs which are available to treat it if it's cancer.
Surely it's worth trying those on endometriosis, isn't it?
Yes, there's definitely a lot of potential there for sure.
The KRAS mutation, as far as I know, it's been a somewhat difficult target.
So the drugs look at, I believe, downstream targets of the KRAS gene.
But we would be very interested in endometriosis of karyosis mutation for specific drugs
and increase the number of treatment options for women.
So a woman listening to this will wonder, should she ask for gene testing if she's got endometriosis?
Is there any point at the moment?
No, at this point, we don't know the full clinical implications of these gene mutations.

So we're actively working on that right now to see whether these mutations influence pain levels or infertility or where endometriosis grows, for example, or whether women will respond to hormonal treatment or surgery.
So all of those are unknowns right now.
And until we know that, mutation testing would be just part of our research protocol.
Paul Young, thank you very much for joining us on The Health Report.

Hip and knee replacements for arthritis are, in the right circumstances, highly effective operations.

The big question, though, is whether by having a joint replacement at a younger age,

There is a register of joint replacements in Australia,

And that's what a study published recently in The Lancet has done,
looking at the effect of age at first total joint replacement on the risk of subsequent revision.

Welcome to The Health Report.

as opposed to the Australian National Joint Replacement Registry,

If you're over 70.
If you're over 70.

there's a significant increase in the risk of a requirement for a second operation.
